title: What you will be able to do
instruction: Press reveal to see each outcome for this lesson.

_items.text: Apply synthesis in your own writing, drawing sources together to form and express your own argument.

title: Beyond analysis and evaluation
body: Analysis takes an interpretation apart. Evaluation weighs it against alternatives. Synthesis is the move that comes after both: putting pieces back together into something that is now your own.

title: What synthesis actually means
body: Dennis and Abbott (2026, pp.128-129) define it as 'the ability to draw together different interpretations or evidence in the formation and expression of your own argument.' Synthesis is not summarising several sources. It is building something new from them.

title: Worked example
body:
Consider two drafts covering the same three sources on the same topic.

{{learner-a}} writes a section source by source: first what Smith argues, then what Jones argues, then what Patel argues.

{{learner-b}} redrafts the same section by grouping the sources around the point each one actually supports, and writes the section around those points, with their own position carrying it.

Both drafts covered the same material. Only {{learner-b}}'s draft was synthesis rather than summary.

title: Why grouping by point changes the writing
body: Once sources are grouped by the point they support, rather than listed in the order you found them, the paragraph has to be organised around your argument instead of around the sources. That reordering is what synthesis actually looks like on the page.

title: Order the stages of synthesis
displayTitle: Put the stages of turning summary into synthesis in order
body: These four stages describe redrafting a section from summary into synthesis, but they are out of sequence.
instruction: Drag items to reorder, or use the keyboard (Enter to grab, arrows to move, Enter to drop). Then select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Put the four stages in order, from first to last.

_items.text: List the sources you currently have, source by source.
Group the sources by the point each one actually supports.
Draft the section organised around those points, not the sources.
Check that your own position is what carries the section.

_feedback.correct: That is the right order. You need the sources listed and grouped before you can draft around the points, and the final check confirms the position is actually yours.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what has to happen before you can draft around points rather than sources.

displayTitle: Two ways to open a synthesis paragraph
body: How you open a paragraph signals whether it will summarise or synthesise.
instruction: Select each tab to compare the two openings.

_items.title: A source-led opening
_items.body: 'Smith (2019) argues that...' This opening commits the paragraph to following Smith's structure, not yours.

_items.title: A point-led opening
_items.body: 'The evidence on this point is mixed.' This opening commits the paragraph to your point, with sources brought in to support it.

title: Redrafting your own work
body: Pick one section you have already written source by source. Group its sources by the point each one makes, then redraft the section around those points. The content barely changes; the argument becomes yours.

title: Your turn
instruction: This is for your own reflection; no right answers are expected.

_items.text: Find a section of your own writing organised source by source. What point could each source be regrouped around?
What would the opening sentence become if the paragraph led with your point instead of a source?
